aions_core/agi_learning.py: This system teaches itself by studying past conversations and improving what it knows. It works like a student reviewing notes after class — when an interaction ends, it examines the question, the answer, and feedback to extract useful patterns and spot gaps in knowledge. The main pieces track learned patterns (the rules it discovers work well), concept relationships (how ideas connect to each other), and interactions (every Q&A it processes). Information flows in as conversations happen, and the system stores what it learns in an SQLite database with separate files for knowledge chunks. It also talks to the core memory system and to Korean compression tools that help it organize information efficiently. The system can consolidate overlapping knowledge, suggest follow-up questions to fill gaps, and generate insights about what works best.
aions_core/memory_graph_engine.py: This file creates a map of how different ideas relate to each other to make searching faster and smarter. Think of it like a spider web where each concept is a point and the threads show which ideas connect. The main pieces load or build a graph from a JSON file, find related concepts by walking those connections, expand a question to include related topics, and assign importance scores to different concepts. It takes in search queries and outputs both expanded searches and tags for categorizing knowledge. The system reads and writes a graph file in JSON format, and it can integrate with the main memory system to improve how it retrieves stored information. When someone searches for a topic, this engine automatically thinks of related topics they might have also meant, making results more complete.
aions_core/server/cbms_direct_server.py: This is a web server that listens for questions and answers them using a compressed memory system. It combines several parts: math solving for arithmetic, pattern matching for common greetings, a memory retrieval system for knowledge-based questions, and a fallback to the internet for topics it does not know. The server accepts chat messages as JSON over HTTP, processes them through multiple routes (math first, then conversational shortcuts, then deep searching), and returns answers as formatted text. It talks to the memory system, a facts database, several optional enhancement modules for making responses more natural, and optionally fetches information from the web. The server tracks performance, quality assurance results, and consciousness patterns if those features are enabled. It runs constantly, waiting for requests on port 9000.
This module makes AI responses sound more natural and human-like instead of robotic or repetitive. It detects what type of question was asked (greeting, emotional, philosophical, creative, technical), and adjusts the response style to match. The main pieces include templates for different response types, emotional context detection, a system to track the conversation history, and synonym replacement to avoid sounding repetitive. The system takes in a basic response and a question, then outputs a warmer, more personalized version that includes appropriate emoticons, natural sentence starters, and context references. It remembers what was discussed before and can reference it later. It also profiles individual users and adapts tone based on their preferences, ranging from formal to casual.
aions_core/server/conversation_memory.py: This file records and recalls conversations to give context for future responses and automatically summarize long discussions. It saves every exchange (question and answer) into date-stamped log files, extracts key topics and names mentioned, and periodically rolls up old summaries into consolidated records. Data flows in as user text and system responses, gets stored in JSON line files organized by session, and gets searched when generating context for new questions. It also detects when users introduce themselves and stores that as a user profile chunk. The system talks to the main memory system to create knowledge chunks from summaries, builds a searchable index of concepts, and rolls up batches of summaries when they reach a certain size. The system helps avoid repeating information and makes conversations feel continuous.
aions_core/tools/bench_runner.py: This testing tool measures how fast the system responds to various types of questions by sending repeated requests and collecting timing data. It submits the same five test queries fifty times each, recording how long each response takes, whether the system refused to answer, and the response size. The raw timing data gets saved as JSON lines in a log file, while a summary calculates median response times (p50) and 95th percentile times (p95) for each query type. It talks to the chat API running on port 9000 and captures both successful responses and error codes. The tool helps detect performance regressions, identifies which questions are slow to answer, and tracks whether the system returns refusals. Results are saved as machine-readable JSON for trend analysis.
aions_core/tools/gsm8k_quick.py: This tool evaluates how well the system solves elementary math word problems by testing it against a standard dataset of twenty questions with known answers. It reads math problems from a test file, sends each one to the chat API, extracts the numeric answer from the response using multiple patterns (looking for the #### format, then answer: format, then the last number in the text), and compares it to the expected answer. It measures both accuracy (percentage correct) and response speed in milliseconds at the 50th and 95th percentile. The system recognizes when it refuses to answer a question and counts those as failures. Results are printed as JSON showing total questions, correct answers, accuracy percentage, refusal count, and timing statistics. This helps verify that the math solving component works correctly and stays fast.
aions_core/tools/query_db.py: This script searches a local SQLite database index to find where specific types of files are stored across the system. It queries the database for JSON files located in chunked storage folders, groups results by parent directory, and reports how many chunks each folder contains in descending order. Data comes from a scan database that indexes files on the hard drive, and results show file paths and counts as plain text output. The tool helps locate where knowledge chunks are physically stored and identifies which folders have the most data. It runs a single SQL query showing the top ten locations by chunk count. This is useful for understanding the structure of stored data and verifying that chunks are being saved where expected.
control_plane/__init__.py: This is a package marker that allows Python to treat the control plane directory as an importable module. The docstring identifies it as the AIONS Control Plane — Phase 3 MVP, marking this as an early version of the coordination system that directs how agents and skills work together. The file contains no runnable code; its sole purpose is to enable imports from this directory so other parts of the system can access the control plane's agents and skill registry components.
control_plane/agents/agent_schema.py: This file defines the structure and validation rules for agent configuration files, ensuring they follow a strict format so agents can run correctly in the system. An agent is like a specialized role that can perform certain skills with specific safety restrictions. The schema requires exact fields: an id starting with agent., a human name and description, which skills it is allowed to use, how much power it has (read-only, can modify, or can delete), which AI model to use, and the system instructions (prompt template). The file loads agent.json files and validates every required field strictly, rejecting the entire agent if anything is missing or wrong. If validation passes, the agent becomes runnable. It rejects agents using fail-closed logic, meaning incomplete configurations never run. This prevents misconfigured agents from causing problems by requiring perfection before they activate.
scripts/catalog_e_treasures.py: This script creates a machine-readable inventory of all the knowledge data and backup copies stored across different hard drives and folders in the system. It scans thirteen different treasure locations, measuring how many files are in each, total size in gigabytes, and how many data packs they contain. It also reads the main knowledge manifest to report how many knowledge chunks are in the active system. The script generates a JSON catalog file with metadata about each treasure location including whether it is currently connected and being used, and notes about its purpose. It outputs the timestamp when the catalog was generated, the generator script name, and summary statistics. This helps understand what data exists where, whether it is archived or active, and how much storage space each collection uses.
scripts/chatgpt_extractor.py: This script reads the ChatGPT Desktop application cache to extract conversation history, custom GPT configurations, and user information. It parses binary LevelDB database files from two cache locations, converts the binary data to readable text, and uses pattern matching to find conversation IDs, titles, timestamps, and message content fragments. It saves results as JSON summary files, plain text chunks, and a markdown report showing all recovered conversations. The script also performs deep extraction by dumping raw cache contents to separate text files to capture any readable strings missed by pattern matching. Data comes from the encrypted ChatGPT cache in Windows AppData, and output goes to a folder with multiple report formats. The tool helps recover conversation history when ChatGPT data needs to be archived or analyzed outside the official application.
scripts/demo_skill_live.py: This demonstration shows how the system learns to combine multiple small actions into reusable recipes and then uses those recipes again instead of planning from scratch. It opens applications, checks if they are already open to avoid repeating actions, runs a multi-step task like finding a file and saving a note about it, verifies the result, and stores that sequence as a reusable recipe. The script loads available skills from a registry, executes them with planning and learning logic, and tracks success statistics. On the second attempt with the same intent, it retrieves the saved recipe instead of replanning. It demonstrates that the system improves with repeated tasks and learns state awareness (knowing when applications are already open). The output shows which skills loaded, execution times, verification results, and whether the system passed by correctly learning and reusing the recipe.
scripts/operator_profile_load.py: This script reads the operator profile file that stores information about who is using the system, loading it from the canonical knowledge storage location. It first tries to find the knowledge directory using an environment variable, then checks standard locations on different drives. If the profile exists, it reads the JSON file and returns the profile data; otherwise, it reports an error. The profile can include information like the operator name, preferences, roles, and other identity information. This helps the system know who it is talking to and can be used to personalize responses or apply user-specific access controls. The script resolves paths across both Windows and Linux-style mount points to work in different environments.
scripts/vault/seal_secret.py: This script encrypts plaintext secret files (like API keys or OAuth credentials) into a secure vault using Windows encryption so only the logged-in operator can read them. It takes a path to a plaintext secret file and a vault identifier, encrypts the file contents using the current Windows user's security key, stores the encrypted blob in the vault directory, and records metadata in an index file. After sealing, the plaintext file should be deleted to prevent accidental exposure. The script warns users never to commit plaintext secrets to git, and instructs agents never to echo file contents. It outputs the vault location, blob filename, and instructions for opening the secret again through a companion script. This protects sensitive credentials like Google OAuth client secrets from being leaked if source code is accidentally shared.
